name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_NUCLEI_MATCH_Q01 - Classification of nuclides by mass and proton numbers

questiontext.text:
Match the nuclear classifications given in List-I with their corresponding defining characteristics given in List-II:

List-I (Classification) List-II (Characteristic)
A. Isotopes I. Nuclei with identical atomic number \(Z\) and identical mass number \(A\), but existing in different nuclear energy states
B. Isobars II. Nuclei with identical atomic number \(Z\), but different neutron number \(N\)
C. Isotones III. Nuclei with identical mass number \(A\), but different atomic number \(Z\)
D. Isomers IV. Nuclei with identical neutron number \(N\), but different atomic number \(Z\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Nuclear Classification
Nuclides are classified into distinct families based on their constituent numbers of protons (\(Z\)), neutrons (\(N\)), mass numbers (\(A = Z + N\)), and internal nuclear energy configurations.

Step 2: Evaluation of Isotopes and Isobars
Isotopes are species of the same chemical element having the same number of protons (\(Z\)), but differing in their neutron number (\(N\)) and consequently having different mass numbers (\(A\)). An example is \(^{1}_{1}\text{H}\), \(^{2}_{1}\text{H}\), and \(^{3}_{1}\text{H}\). Therefore, isotopes correspond to nuclei with identical atomic number \(Z\), but different neutron number \(N\).
Isobars are nuclides possessing the same total mass number (\(A\)), but different atomic numbers (\(Z\)) and neutron numbers (\(N\)). Examples include \(^{3}_{1}\text{H}\) and \(^{3}_{2}\text{He}\), both having \(A = 3\). Therefore, isobars correspond to nuclei with identical mass number \(A\), but different atomic number \(Z\).

Step 3: Evaluation of Isotones and Nuclear Isomers
Isotones are nuclides containing an identical number of neutrons (\(N = A - Z\)), but having different atomic numbers (\(Z\)) and different mass numbers (\(A\)). An example pair is \(^{198}_{80}\text{Hg}\) and \(^{197}_{79}\text{Au}\), both possessing \(N = 118\). Therefore, isotones correspond to nuclei with identical neutron number \(N\), but different atomic number \(Z\).
Nuclear isomers are metastable nuclear states possessing identical atomic number \(Z\) and identical mass number \(A\), but differing in internal excitation energies, half-lives, and radioactive decay modes. Therefore, isomers correspond to nuclei with identical atomic number \(Z\) and identical mass number \(A\), but existing in different nuclear energy states.

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Pairing
Reviewing each pair systematically confirms that isotopes correspond to identical \(Z\) with differing \(N\); isobars correspond to identical \(A\) with differing \(Z\); isotones correspond to identical \(N\) with differing \(Z\); and isomers correspond to identical \(Z\) and \(A\) with differing nuclear energy states.

Final Answer:
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-III, C-IV, D-I.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_NUCLEI_MATCH_Q02 - Discoveries and theoretical models in nuclear physics

questiontext.text:
Match the scientists listed in List-I with their pioneering contributions to nuclear physics listed in List-II:

List-I (Scientist) List-II (Contribution)
A. James Chadwick I. Discovery of the dense atomic nucleus via \(\alpha\)-particle scattering experiments
B. Ernest Rutherford II. Discovery of the uncharged constituent of the nucleus, the neutron
C. Albert Einstein III. Formulation of the meson exchange theory of strong nuclear interactions
D. Hideki Yukawa IV. Formulation of the mass-energy equivalence principle, \(E = mc^2\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Nuclear Discoveries and Models
The development of modern nuclear physics relies on foundational experimental discoveries and theoretical frameworks governing nuclear composition, mass-energy balance, and binding forces.

Step 2: Evaluation of Chadwick and Rutherford
James Chadwick in 1932 bombarded beryllium with \(\alpha\)-particles and observed neutral radiation that ejected protons from paraffin. He established that this neutral radiation consisted of neutral particles of mass nearly equal to that of a proton, thereby discovering the neutron. Hence, James Chadwick corresponds to the discovery of the uncharged constituent of the nucleus, the neutron.
Ernest Rutherford, through the famous Geiger-Marsden \(\alpha\)-particle scattering experiment in 1911, observed that a small fraction of \(\alpha\)-particles suffered large deflections and even rebounds, concluding that the entire positive charge and almost all mass of the atom are concentrated in a tiny central region called the nucleus. Hence, Ernest Rutherford corresponds to the discovery of the dense atomic nucleus via \(\alpha\)-particle scattering experiments.

Step 3: Evaluation of Einstein and Yukawa
Albert Einstein established the special theory of relativity in 1905, from which the mass-energy equivalence relation \(E = mc^2\) emerges, forming the fundamental basis for calculating mass defects, nuclear binding energies, and the energy released in nuclear reactions. Hence, Albert Einstein corresponds to the formulation of the mass-energy equivalence principle, \(E = mc^2\).
Hideki Yukawa in 1935 proposed that the strong, short-range nuclear forces holding nucleons together within the nucleus arise from the virtual exchange of intermediate-mass bosons known as mesons (specifically \(\pi\)-mesons or pions). Hence, Hideki Yukawa corresponds to the formulation of the meson exchange theory of strong nuclear interactions.

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Pairing
Verification confirms that Chadwick discovered the neutron; Rutherford discovered the atomic nucleus; Einstein formulated mass-energy equivalence; and Yukawa proposed the meson exchange theory of strong nuclear forces.

Final Answer:
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_NUCLEI_MATCH_Q03 - Characteristic features of different fundamental nuclear processes

questiontext.text:
Match each nuclear process listed in List-I with its defining characteristic reaction or feature listed in List-II:

List-I (Nuclear Process) List-II (Defining Feature / Reaction)
A. Induced nuclear fission I. Spontaneous decay of an isolated nucleon outside the nucleus into a proton, electron, and antineutrino
B. Thermonuclear fusion II. Thermal neutron capture by a heavy nucleus leading to splitting into two intermediate-mass fragments with a release of approximately \(200\text{ MeV}\)
C. Free neutron decay III. Combining of four protons through cyclic catalytic steps to form a helium-4 nucleus with a net release of about \(26.7\text{ MeV}\)
D. Deuteron-deuteron reaction IV. Direct collision of two light hydrogen isotopes producing tritium and a proton or helium-3 and a neutron with releases around \(3.27\text{ to }4.03\text{ MeV}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Nuclear Transformations
Nuclear transformations encompass processes where the binding energy per nucleon changes significantly, releasing kinetic energy and producing characteristic daughter products.

Step 2: Evaluation of Induced Fission and Thermonuclear Fusion
In induced nuclear fission, an incident thermal neutron is captured by a fissile heavy nuclide such as \(^{235}_{92}\text{U}\), forming an unstable compound nucleus \(^{236}_{92}\text{U}^*\) that splits into two lighter fragments (such as barium and krypton) along with \(2\) to \(3\) fast neutrons and an average energy release of about \(200\text{ MeV}\). Hence, induced nuclear fission corresponds to thermal neutron capture by a heavy nucleus leading to splitting into two intermediate-mass fragments with a release of approximately \(200\text{ MeV}\).
In thermonuclear fusion inside stars (such as the Sun), four protons undergo the proton-proton chain cycle at extreme temperatures and pressures, yielding one \(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\) nucleus, two positrons, two electron neutrinos, and about \(26.7\text{ MeV}\) of energy. Hence, thermonuclear fusion corresponds to the combining of four protons through cyclic catalytic steps to form a helium-4 nucleus with a net release of about \(26.7\text{ MeV}\).

Step 3: Evaluation of Free Neutron Decay and Deuteron-Deuteron Fusion
An isolated, free neutron is unstable against weak interaction beta-decay, having a mean lifetime of approximately \(1000\text{ s}\) and decaying according to \(n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e\). Hence, free neutron decay corresponds to the spontaneous decay of an isolated nucleon outside the nucleus into a proton, electron, and antineutrino.
In laboratory or fusion reactor conditions, two deuterium nuclei (\(^{2}_{1}\text{H}\)) can fuse via two equally probable branches: \(^{2}_{1}\text{H} + {^{2}_{1}\text{H}} \rightarrow {^{3}_{2}\text{He}} + n + 3.27\text{ MeV}\), or \(^{2}_{1}\text{H} + {^{2}_{1}\text{H}} \rightarrow {^{3}_{1}\text{H}} + p + 4.03\text{ MeV}\). Hence, the deuteron-deuteron reaction corresponds to the direct collision of two light hydrogen isotopes producing tritium and a proton or helium-3 and a neutron with releases around \(3.27\text{ to }4.03\text{ MeV}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Pairing
Comparing all four items validates that induced fission releases \(\approx 200\text{ MeV}\) via heavy-nucleus splitting; stellar thermonuclear fusion yields \(\approx 26.7\text{ MeV}\) via hydrogen-to-helium conversion; free neutron decay produces a proton, electron, and antineutrino; and deuteron-deuteron fusion yields tritium/helium-3 with \(3.27\) to \(4.03\text{ MeV}\).

Final Answer:
The correct matching sequence is A-II, B-III, C-I, D-IV.

name.text: NEET_UG_PHYSICS_NUCLEI_MATCH_Q04 - Characteristic numerical scales and physical constants of nuclei

questiontext.text:
Match the physical parameters and characteristic nuclear constants given in List-I with their accepted standard values given in List-II:

List-I (Nuclear Parameter / Constant) List-II (Standard Value)
A. Constant in the nuclear radius formula, \(R_0\) I. Approximately \(2.3 \times 10^{17}\text{ kg m}^{-3}\)
B. Internucleon separation for minimum nuclear potential energy, \(r_0\) II. Approximately \(8.75\text{ MeV per nucleon}\)
C. Average density of nuclear matter, \(\rho_{\text{nucl}}\) III. Approximately \(1.2\text{ fm}\)
D. Maximum binding energy per nucleon, \(E_{bn}\) (for \(^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}\)) IV. Approximately \(0.8\text{ fm}\)

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principles of Nuclear Scales and Parameters
Nuclear structure is characterized by precise microscopic dimensions, nuclear matter density, internucleon potential profiles, and binding energy per nucleon maxima described in standard nuclear physics.

Step 2: Evaluation of Radius Constant and Separation for Minimum Potential
The nuclear radius is experimentally established through electron scattering and alpha scattering to obey the empirical relationship \(R = R_0 A^{1/3}\), where the constant of proportionality \(R_0\) is approximately \(1.2 \times 10^{-15}\text{ m} = 1.2\text{ fm}\). Hence, the constant in the nuclear radius formula corresponds to approximately \(1.2\text{ fm}\).
The potential energy curve between two nucleons plotted as a function of separation distance \(r\) shows that the nuclear force is strongly repulsive at extremely small distances and becomes strongly attractive at distances around \(1\text{ fm}\). The potential energy possesses a distinct minimum at an equilibrium separation \(r_0 \approx 0.8\text{ fm}\). Hence, the internucleon separation for minimum nuclear potential energy corresponds to approximately \(0.8\text{ fm}\).

Step 3: Evaluation of Nuclear Density and Maximum Binding Energy per Nucleon
Nuclear mass density is determined by dividing the mass of the nucleus (\(m A\)) by its spherical volume (\(\frac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = \frac{4}{3}\pi R_0^3 A\)):
\[\rho_{\text{nucl}} = \frac{3m}{4\pi R_0^3} \approx \frac{3 \times 1.66 \times 10^{-27}}{4\pi \times (1.2 \times 10^{-15})^3} \approx 2.3 \times 10^{17}\text{ kg m}^{-3}\]
Because the mass number \(A\) cancels completely, this extraordinarily high density is independent of nuclear size. Hence, the average density of nuclear matter corresponds to approximately \(2.3 \times 10^{17}\text{ kg m}^{-3}\).
On the binding energy per nucleon (\(E_{bn}\)) versus mass number (\(A\)) curve, the binding energy per nucleon reaches its maximum value of approximately \(8.75\text{ MeV per nucleon}\) for iron-56 (\(^{56}_{26}\text{Fe}\)), representing the most tightly bound and stable nuclide. Hence, the maximum binding energy per nucleon corresponds to approximately \(8.75\text{ MeV per nucleon}\).

Step 4: Check and Final Conceptual Pairing
Cross-checking each assignment confirms that the radius parameter is \(1.2\text{ fm}\); the potential minimum separation is \(0.8\text{ fm}\); the nuclear matter density is \(2.3 \times 10^{17}\text{ kg m}^{-3}\); and the peak binding energy per nucleon is \(8.75\text{ MeV per nucleon}\).

Final Answer:
The correct matching sequence is A-III, B-IV, C-I, D-II.
